headline: Proximie has 100+ TB of theatre video and a new NHS/AWS/Deloitte pilot that must turn it into phase and instrument labels fast, but almost all of it is redundant footage that clinician annotators should never see.
what_they_build: Proximie is an OR operating system: hardware plus cloud that records, streams and stores surgery from 500+ facilities, sold to hospital groups (NHS trusts) and 40+ medical device companies. The Intelligence Suite applies computer vision to that footage to measure throughput, utilisation and workflow; the Surgical Suite builds the video library for training and quality. Buyers pay for theatre capacity and for medtech product adoption insight.
inferred_pipeline: Theatre hardware captures laparoscopic feed plus room cameras, with on-device computer vision used for privacy masking before upload (stated on site).
Video lands in Proximie's cloud, most likely AWS S3 given the AWS pilot; roughly 100+ TB and growing (guess on volume split between room and scope video).
Clips are selected for AI work by procedure type or by whoever asks, rather than by frame-level quality or diversity metrics (guess, no evidence of a curation layer).
Labelling of surgical phase, instruments and theatre milestones is done by a mix of clinical reviewers and an outsourced vendor, possibly inside a tool built in-house or via Deloitte (guess).
Models for phase recognition and utilisation timestamps are trained and evaluated offline, with aggregate accuracy reported rather than per-procedure or per-site slices (guess).
Outputs feed Intelligence Suite dashboards for throughput and turnaround time at each trust.

hypotheses.pain: Clinician annotator time is the bottleneck. Phase and instrument labelling on long, mostly uneventful surgical video means surgeons and scrub nurses watch hours of footage to produce a few useful labels.
hypotheses.evidence: 100+ TB of video and 80k recorded views on the site; the NHS pilot is framed as the largest AI theatre evaluation, so label volume steps up sharply.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Index ranks frames by quality and uniqueness and clusters by embedding, so reviewers only see the diverse 30-40%. Annotate adds native video timelines, frame classifications for phase and object tracking with interpolation for instruments. Our own test cut frames to label by 61% keeping 95% of scenes.

hypotheses.pain: Proving theatre capacity gains to NHS trusts needs per-site, per-procedure accuracy evidence, not a single aggregate number, and failures will cluster in poor lighting, smoke and out-of-body frames.
hypotheses.evidence: The AWS and Deloitte pilot is positioned around unlocking hidden operating theatre capacity across 104+ theatres, which implies per-trust reporting and scrutiny.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Active imports your predictions and gives mAP, F1, PR curves and confusion matrix sliced by class, site or any data metric such as brightness and sharpness. Metric-to-failure correlation then tells you which footage to label next instead of labelling more of the same.

hypotheses.pain: Patient and staff identifiability in room video makes any external labelling workforce or tool a governance problem, slowing IG approval with each new trust.
hypotheses.evidence: Site stresses low-bandwidth hardware with built-in computer vision to protect privacy, and the pilot runs on NHS patient data.
hypotheses.encord_answer: Index registers data from your own AWS bucket, the files never move to us. SOC2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR, and Agents can run your own redaction or out-of-body detector as a workflow stage so nothing identifiable reaches a human reviewer.

ontology.name: Surgical phase
ontology.why: Core label for workflow timing and throughput analysis across a procedure.

ontology.name: Out-of-body / non-clinical frame
ontology.why: Gates privacy risk and removes scope-out footage before human review.

ontology.name: Surgical instrument
ontology.why: Instrument presence and usage drives phase inference and medtech adoption metrics.

ontology.name: Instrument tip
ontology.why: Tracks motion and dexterity for training and skills assessment.

ontology.name: Anatomy / critical structure
ontology.why: Fine boundaries needed for critical view of safety style checks.

ontology.name: Identifiable person or screen region
ontology.why: Validates redaction coverage for faces, badges and monitors in room video.

ontology.name: Adverse event (bleeding, smoke)
ontology.why: Rare-event mining and a known source of model failure.

ontology.name: Theatre milestone (patient in, incision, closure, patient out)
ontology.why: Direct input to utilisation and turnaround time reporting for trusts.

case_study.name: Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital
case_study.why_it_matches: Clinical experts doing the annotation, PHI-sensitive imaging, and the same problem of expert minutes being the scarce resource. For the curation side, Automotus is the closer analogue: continuous camera streams where most frames are near duplicates.
case_study.numbers: Harvard/MGH: annotation time cut from days to minutes. Automotus: +20% mAP on a 35% smaller dataset with 33% lower labelling cost after curating in Encord.

proof_of_value: Week 1, day 1-2: register one de-identified procedure set (target 50-100 hours of video) from Proximie's own AWS bucket in Index. No data movement. Success: embeddings and quality metrics computed, browsable by brightness, sharpness and uniqueness.

Week 1, day 3-5: build a Collection that drops out-of-body and near-duplicate frames and samples for diversity across sites and procedure types. Success: agreed target of 50-60% reduction in frames sent to clinical reviewers while retaining 95% of distinct phases.

Week 2, day 1-2: stand up the phase and instrument ontology in Annotate with a review workflow, and wire an Agent running Proximie's existing phase or redaction model as a pre-labelling stage. Success: measured minutes per procedure-hour for a reviewer versus their current tool.
Week 2, day 3-4: import Proximie's current model predictions into Active and slice performance by phase, site and lighting metrics. Success: a named list of the three data slices driving most errors.

Week 2, day 5: train or fine-tune on the curated pick versus a random pick of equal size and compare. Success criterion agreed up front, for example equal or better phase accuracy on half the labelled frames.
discovery_questions: For the NHS pilot, how many hours of theatre video do you expect to need labelled, and who actually does the labelling today, clinicians, an outsourced team or Deloitte?
What tool are your annotators in right now, and did you build it or buy it?
How do you currently decide which clips get labelled next, and how much of what you label turns out to be near-identical footage?
When a trust challenges a utilisation number, how do you show accuracy for that site and that procedure type specifically?
Where does the de-identification step happen, on the hardware or in the cloud, and what would have to be true for a labelling platform to sit alongside your AWS environment?
risks: AWS and Deloitte are already in the room; labelling may be scoped into the SI contract or defaulted to SageMaker Ground Truth as part of the pilot's cloud credits.
On-device computer vision in their hardware suggests real in-house CV capability, so they may have built their own annotation and review tooling already.
NHS information governance on patient video could make even a bring-your-own-bucket deployment a multi-month approval, longer than the pilot window.
Around $11m estimated ARR means tooling budget is tight and likely tied to the pilot's funding rather than a standing platform line.
